nodes.title: Katz cyclic-vector candidate
nodes.statement: For a rank-n differential module with ordered basis e₀,…,eₙ₋₁ over R, define c(e,x)=Σ₀≤j<n (x^j/j!) Σ₀≤k≤j (−1)^k binom(j,k) D^k(e_(j−k)). The rank-zero candidate is zero. This is an explicit candidate, not an assertion that every x works.
hypotheses: R is a commutative differential ring; D is additive and satisfies D(rv)=∂(r)v+rD(v).
(n−1)! is invertible when n>0; x=t−a with ∂t=1 and ∂a=0 for the cyclic-vector theorem.
proofSteps: Form the finite sums on the existing module carrier; keep the connection constant-linear.
Use the binomial cancellation in its first n differential jets; do not define cyclicity again, since the main packet already owns it.

nodes.title: Katz determinant criterion
nodes.statement: With ∂t=1 put c_i(e,X)=Σ_(j<n)(X^j/j!)c(i,j), where c(0,j) is the inner sum of the candidate (zero for j≥n) and c(i+1,j)=D(c(i,j))+c(i,j+1); equivalently c_i(e,X)=D^i c(e,X) for the candidate over R[X] with ∂X=1. Then c₀∧⋯∧c_(n−1)=P(X)e₀∧⋯∧e_(n−1) for a polynomial P∈R[X] with P(0)=1 and degree at most n(n−1), and for a constant a the vector c(e,t−a) is cyclic if and only if P(t−a) is a unit.
hypotheses: n>0; (n−1)! invertible; R commutative; e a basis; the connection extends to R[X] by Leibniz.
proofSteps: Induction on i+j gives c(i,j)=Σ_k(−1)^k binom(j,k)D^k(e_(i+j−k)) for i+j≤n−1, so c(i,0)=eᵢ and c_i(e,0)=eᵢ: the coordinate matrix at X=0 is the identity.
Each jet column has X-degree at most n−1, so the determinant has degree at most n(n−1).
Specialisation at X=t−a commutes with D exactly when a is constant. Invertibility of the determinant is the basis criterion.

sources.locator: Proofs of Theorems 1–2, pp. 66–67
sources.match: Katz's proof of Theorem 1 gives c(i,0)=eᵢ (p. 66); the proof of Theorem 2 gives the polynomial P with P(0)=1, degree at most n(n−1), and the equivalence between cyclicity of c(e,t−a) and P(t−a)∈R^× (p. 67).

acceptance: The Wronskian at X=0 is 1, not merely nonzero.
Track the differential structure on the polynomial variable; ordinary coefficientwise differentiation would fail.

nodes.title: Katz cyclic-vector algorithm
nodes.statement: If R is local and t−a lies in its maximal ideal, c(e,t−a) is cyclic. More generally, if constants contain a field k with at least N=n(n−1)+1 elements, any N distinct constants aᵢ yield candidates whose cyclic loci cover Spec R. Over a differential field of characteristic zero with ∂t=1, at least one of these candidates is cyclic.
hypotheses: n>0; finite free rank n; the factorial assumption of katz-candidate.
For the global conclusion k⊂ker ∂ is a field and N pairwise distinct aᵢ belong to k.
proofSteps: Locally the determinant reduces to 1 modulo the maximal ideal.
Globally evaluate P at t−aᵢ. The Vandermonde determinant is a product of nonzero constant differences, hence a unit.
Since P has degree ≤N−1 and constant term 1, its coefficients, and therefore the evaluation values, generate the unit ideal. Each prime admits an invertible evaluation after localisation.

sources.locator: Theorems 1–2 and proofs, pp. 65–67
sources.match: The field proof is obtained from a finite covering by explicit candidates, not by an unspecified generic vector.

acceptance: Use exactly N candidates, including N=1 in rank one.
The conclusion over a ring is local cyclicity, not necessarily one globally cyclic candidate.

nodes.title: Rescaling a nonzero derivation
nodes.statement: Over a characteristic-zero differential field with ∂≠0, choose t with s=∂t≠0. Put δ=s⁻¹∂ and D′=s⁻¹D. For every v, the spans of the first n iterates of D and D′ agree; cyclicity is unchanged. Hence the Katz algorithm applies with δt=1.
hypotheses: K a characteristic-zero field; D constant-linear with Leibniz rule; n is the finite rank.
proofSteps: Use the Leibniz rule to check D′ is a connection for δ.
Induction gives (D′)^i(v)=s^(−i)D^i(v) plus lower iterates. The transition matrix is triangular with nonzero diagonal.
Apply the finite-candidate theorem. With ∂=0 and D=0 on K² no vector is cyclic; do not drop ∂≠0.

sources.locator: pp. 65–67, ∂t=1 setup; rescaling argument supplied here
sources.match: The argument explicitly connects the normalised algorithm to the main cyclic-vector statement.

acceptance: The field hypothesis is needed to invert s.

nodes.title: Rational-type differential fields and intrinsic radii for several derivations
nodes.statement: Let K be a complete nonarchimedean field of characteristic 0 and residue characteristic p, with commuting derivations ∂₁,…,∂ₘ. A derivation ∂ is of rational type with parameter u if ∂(u)=1, |∂|_K=|u|⁻¹ and |∂ⁿ/n!|_K≤|∂|_Kⁿ for all n≥1 (equivalently |∂|_sp,K=ω|∂|_K, ω=p^(−1/(p−1))); K is of rational type for u₁,…,uₘ if each ∂ⱼ is of rational type with parameter uⱼ and ∂ᵢ(uⱼ)=0 for i≠j. A ∂ⱼ-differential module is a finite projective K-module with an action of ∂ⱼ alone; a ∂_J-differential module carries commuting actions of all ∂ⱼ. For nonzero V the extrinsic ∂ⱼ-radius is R_∂ⱼ(V)=ω|∂ⱼ|_sp,V⁻¹, the intrinsic ∂ⱼ-radius is IR_∂ⱼ(V)=|∂ⱼ|_sp,K/|∂ⱼ|_sp,V=|uⱼ|R_∂ⱼ(V)∈(0,1], and the intrinsic radius is IR(V)=min_j IR_∂ⱼ(V); ∂ⱼ is dominant for V if IR_∂ⱼ(V)=IR(V). The intrinsic subsidiary radii IR(V;1)≤…≤IR(V;dim V) list the intrinsic radii of the Jordan–Hölder constituents with multiplicity; V has pure intrinsic radii if they are all equal. On a disc or annulus the profiles use F_η, the completion of K(t) for the η-Gauss norm, which is of rational type for ∂₀=d/dt (parameter t) together with ∂₁,…,∂ₘ.
hypotheses: Residue characteristic p>0 for the targets here; the definitions also make sense for p=0, where ω=1.
Spectral norms are computed for any norm on V compatible with K; they do not depend on that choice.
proofSteps: Rational type is KX Definition 1.4.1; the equivalence of the factorial bound with |∂|_sp,K=ω|∂|_K is KX Corollary 1.2.13, and Remark 1.4.2 gives |∂ⁿ/n!|_K=|u|^(−n) and IR_∂(V)=|u|R_∂(V).
Several derivations: KX Definitions 1.5.1–1.5.3; F_η is again of rational type for ∂₀,…,∂ₘ (KX Remark 1.5.4).

Taylor map: for each derivation the series x↦Σ_s ∂^s(x)T^s/s! is a continuous homomorphism, isometric for the Gauss norms of radius at most the parameter's absolute value (KX Lemma 1.2.12); for commuting derivations the multivariable series is the composite. Generic rotation uses this map.
For ∂₀=d/dt on F_η the intrinsic radius is R(E,η)/η, the main packet's toric radius T(E,η); this fixes the compatibility with generic-radius.

nodes.title: Frobenius antecedents and descendants for a rational-type derivation
nodes.statement: Let ∂ be of rational type on K with parameter u, p>0. The ∂-Frobenius ϕ^(∂)*:K^(∂)↪K is the inclusion of the fixed field of the action i↦(x↦Σ_s ∂^s(x)((ζ_p^i−1)u)^s/s!) of Z/pZ (by Galois descent when ζ_p∉K); K^(∂) carries ∂′=∂/(pu^(p−1)), of rational type with parameter u^p. For a ∂-differential module V, the descendant ϕ^(∂)_*V (restriction of scalars, with ∂′) has intrinsic subsidiary radii obtained by replacing each r∈IR_∂(V) by r^p together with p^(−p/(p−1)) (p−1 times) if r>p^(−1/(p−1)), and by p^(−1)r (p times) if r≤p^(−1/(p−1)). If IR_∂(V)>p^(−1/(p−1)) there is a unique ∂′-module V′ with V≅ϕ^(∂)*V′ and IR_∂′(V′)>p^(−p/(p−1)), and then IR_∂′(V′)=IR_∂(V)^p. For V′ with IR_∂′(V′)≠p^(−p/(p−1)), IR_∂(ϕ^(∂)*V′)=min{IR_∂′(V′)^(1/p), p·IR_∂′(V′)}. With several derivations the others remain of rational type on K^(∂ⱼ).
hypotheses: K is a complete nonarchimedean characteristic-zero field, with positive residue characteristic p, commuting rational-type coefficient derivations ∂₁,…,∂ₘ and parameters uⱼ (rational-type-intrinsic-radii). KX Hypothesis 2.0.1 also allows residue characteristic 0; that case is not needed here.
p>0; V is a nonzero finite-dimensional ∂-differential module.
proofSteps: KX Lemmas 1.4.8–1.4.9 compute |∂′|=|u|^(−p) and show ∂′ is of rational type with parameter u^p; their proofs are in KX.
The antecedent (KX Proposition 1.4.17) is proved as in book Theorem 10.4.2; the descendant radii (KX Theorem 1.4.19) as in book Theorem 10.5.1. These book proofs are part of gap G1.

Corollary 1.4.20 follows from Theorem 1.4.19 and the decomposition ϕ^(∂)*ϕ^(∂)_*V′≅⊕_(n<p)V′⊗W_n of KX Lemma 1.4.15(d), where W_n is the line with ∂′v=(n/p)u^(−p)v and IR_∂′(W_n)=p^(−p/(p−1)) for n≠0.

For ∂=d/dt in the coordinate t this is the main packet's Christol–Dwork antecedent (frobenius-antecedent); the coefficient derivations need this rational-type version, since the main node is stated for the coordinate t of an annulus, whereas K^(∂ⱼ) is the fixed field of a Z/pZ-action on a general rational-type field.

nodes.title: Decomposition by intrinsic radii over a rational-type field
nodes.statement: Let K be of rational type for ∂₁,…,∂ₘ. Every ∂_J-differential module V over K decomposes as V=⊕_(r∈(0,1]) V_r, where every subquotient of V_r has pure intrinsic radii r; for one derivation this is the decomposition by intrinsic ∂-radii. If p=0 then r^(dim V_r)∈|K^×|; if p>0 and h≥0, then r<p^(−p^(−h)/(p−1)) implies r^(dim V_r)∈|K^×|^(1/p^h).
hypotheses: K complete nonarchimedean of characteristic 0, of rational type for u₁,…,uₘ; any residue characteristic.
V a finite-dimensional ∂_J-differential module; the decomposition is by ∂_J-submodules and is unique.
proofSteps: One derivation: below the visibility bound this is Robba's decomposition (robba-factorization-and-radius-decomposition); beyond it, iterate Frobenius descendants (partial-frobenius-descendant) as in book Theorems 10.6.2 and 10.7.1, which KX cite for Theorem 1.4.21 (gap G1). The value-group statement comes from the Newton-polygon slopes.

Several derivations: each ∂ⱼ-decomposition is stable under every ∂ᵢ, since the projection of ∂ᵢ(V_r) to V_(r′) is K-linear and ∂ⱼ-equivariant between modules with disjoint radii, hence zero; take the common refinement (KX's proof of Theorem 1.5.6).

sources.locator: Theorem 1.4.21 and Remark 1.4.22, p. 15; Theorem 1.5.6 and proof, p. 16
sources.match: KX state the decomposition by intrinsic radii for one rational-type derivation and deduce it for several by a common refinement.

nodes.title: Extrinsic subsidiary-radius variation
nodes.statement: For the ∂₀-connection, order subsidiary radii R₁≤…≤R_d; set fᵢ(r)=−log Rᵢ(M,e^(−r)) and Fᵢ=Σⱼ≤i fⱼ. All fᵢ and Fᵢ are continuous and piecewise affine; Fᵢ is convex, and its affine slopes are integral whenever i=d or fᵢ>fᵢ₊₁. In general slopes of fᵢ lie in the union of (1/e)ℤ for 1≤e≤d. On a disc, slopes of Fᵢ are nonpositive where fᵢ>r, and fᵢ=r for sufficiently large r.

nodes.title: Kedlaya monodromy key calculation
nodes.statement: In the algebraically closed extended analytic ring with invertible q-Frobenius σ fixing a uniformiser π, let n≥1 and x=Σᵢ₌₀ⁿuᵢπ^i, where the uᵢ are strong semiunits of negative residue valuation or zero and x≠0. There exist a,b, not both zero, with σ(a)=πa and πσ^n(b)=b−ax.
hypotheses: The extended-ring topology, strong-semiunit partial valuations and Frobenius action are those of RD.0.
The residue valuation is nontrivial; complete algebraically closed residue field; π is fixed by σ.
Normalise the π-adic contribution to w_ρ so w_ρ(π)=1 in the nonvanishing calculation.
proofSteps: For m>0 set f(i,l,m)=(v₀(uᵢ)+m q^(−l))q^(−n(i+l)), and h(m)=minᵢ,ₗ f(i,l,m). The minimum is locally finite, increasing, piecewise affine, and h(qm)=q^(−n)h(m). Choose a corner τ with h(τ)<0.
Define T by f(i,l,τ)<0, S by f(i,l,τ)<q^(−n)h(τ), and s(i,l)=floor(log_(q^n)(h(τ)/f(i,l,τ))). S is finite; s≥0, and only finitely many indices have bounded s.

On the uniformly bounded partial-valuation modules U_τ→U_h(τ), define the additive π-linear convergent operator r(z)=Σ_T π^s σ^(−ni−nl+ns)(uᵢ) σ^(−ni−(n+1)l+ns)(z). Its reduction is a finite Puiseux polynomial with distinct exponents. The corner supplies a nonzero root of valuation τ.

Lift every required reduction recursively modulo successive powers of π, keeping the same uniform valuation bound. Completeness and continuity then give a nonzero z with v₀(z)=τ and r(z)=0; dense image alone would not imply surjectivity.

Put a=Σₗ∈ℤπ^lσ^(−l)(z). Since z∈U_τ and v₀(z)=τ, w_ρ(π^lσ^(−l)(z))=l+ρq^(−l)τ. Choose 1/(q−1)<ρτ<q/(q−1): the l=0 term uniquely minimises the valuation, so a≠0. The valuations tend to infinity at both ends and σ(a)=πa. Split ax=A+B using T; B has nonnegative partial valuation. The nonnegative-valuation difference input (monodromy Proposition 3.19(d), pp. 126–127) writes B=πσ^n(b₁)−b₁: explicitly b₁=−Σₖ≥0π^kσ^(nk)(B). Nonnegative residue partial valuations and the increasing π powers guarantee its convergence, and finite sums telescope.

For each index in T, the oriented finite geometric sum of length i+l−s gives b₂ (the source writes an ordinary sum from j=1 to i+l−s, but i+l−s can be negative for small corners, so the oriented convention is needed for its telescoping identity: source issue E310) with A=r(z)+πσ^n(b₂)−b₂. The integers i+l−s are uniformly bounded, so all summation k lie in one finite set of integers. Each unshifted summand has every partial valuation ≥h(τ), and σ^(nk) multiplies this bound by one of finitely many q^(nk). The π shifts have a uniform lower index bound; bounded-s index sets are finite. These facts give a uniform residue-valuation lower bound, π-adic convergence and overconvergence. Set b=−b₁−b₂; since a≠0 the pair is nonzero. G2 records only the ordinary Newton-polygon supplier still missing.

nodes.title: Descending bounded generic slope filtration
nodes.statement: Every finite-dimensional Frobenius module M over E† has a unique filtration by saturated Frobenius submodules whose completed graded pieces are isoclinic of strictly decreasing arithmetic slopes. The filtration completes to the decreasing generic slope filtration over E. If F is algebraically closed, every graded piece is a direct sum of standard E† blocks of its one slope; M itself need not be their direct sum.
hypotheses: F is a perfect complete nontrivially valued characteristic-p field; q is a power of p; σ raises residue coefficients to q-th powers and fixes π.
E† is the bounded overconvergent Teichmüller coefficient field and E its π-adic completion, in the Fargues–Fontaine §11.2.5 convention; the coefficient-ring identification is requested from RD.0.
Frobenius modules have invertible linearisation; this does not imply Frobenius is bijective on an arbitrary integral lattice.

The argument is Kedlaya's, proved in the monodromy paper for a perfect algebraic extension of k((t)) (a 'valued field' there, §2.2, p. 102); for FF's complete perfect F the Galois-descent step uses FF Proposition 11.2.15 and the extended-ring step is SFR Proposition 5.4.3 (any K). This extension of Kedlaya's setting is part of the coefficient-ring comparison G3.
proofSteps: Take the highest completed slope submodule. Its determinant is a rank-one Frobenius line in an exterior power.

In rank one choose λ with the highest slope and a completed eigenbasis vᵢ. Approximate it by bounded overconvergent wᵢ so λwᵢ=ΣⱼBᵢⱼF(wⱼ), with B mod π=diag(1,0,…,0). For v₁=Σcᵢwᵢ use σ(cᵢ)=ΣⱼBⱼᵢcⱼ. Choose r with w_r(B)≥0; induction in the π-index gives rv_h(cᵢ)+h≥0. At h=0 the coordinates reduce to δᵢ₁, not all to zero. Thus the determinant line has overconvergent coordinates. Apply the imported saturated exterior-power descent and the RD.0 intersection statement to descend from the algebraic extension.

Pass to the quotient and induct on rank. Completed uniqueness and injectivity give uniqueness over E†. For the graded standard forms when F is algebraically closed, apply the fixed-slope completion comparison (isoclinic-completion-comparison) to each isoclinic graded piece; the source instead repeats the eigenvector descent on each piece and applies its Proposition 5.3. Full faithfulness on mixed slopes is never used.

nodes.title: Bijective integral-lattice invariant descent
nodes.statement: If Λ is finite free over O_E† and Frobenius is bijective on Λ (matrix A∈GL_n(O_E†)), then Λ^(σ=1)→(Λ⊗O_E)^(σ=1) is an isomorphism.
hypotheses: F is a perfect complete nontrivially valued characteristic-p field; q is a power of p; σ raises residue coefficients to q-th powers and fixes π.
E† is the bounded overconvergent Teichmüller coefficient field and E its π-adic completion, in the Fargues–Fontaine §11.2.5 convention; the coefficient-ring identification is requested from RD.0.
Frobenius modules have invertible linearisation; this does not imply Frobenius is bijective on an arbitrary integral lattice.
The integral Frobenius matrix and its inverse have integral entries; fixed vectors are integral.
proofSteps: A fixed vector satisfies X=Aσ(X), so σ(X)=A⁻¹X. Apply the coefficient estimates to B=A⁻¹.
Rescale the basis by a Teichmüller scalar of sufficiently large residue norm so the reduction of B has entries in O_F. Choose one small positive radius ρ₀ with the resulting partial seminorm bound.

Iterate σ(X)=BX in each truncation. Frobenius scales the residue norm exponent by q; the first nonzero π-index bounds all truncations at the same ρ₀. Thus the coordinates are overconvergent. Injectivity is inclusion.
The matrix [[1,0],[c,π]] with |c|>1 violates integral bijectivity and has a completed fixed vector e₁+Σⱼ≥0π^j[c^(q^j)]e₂ that is not overconvergent.

nodes.title: Negative-slope Frobenius cokernel comparison
nodes.statement: For d>0 and h≥1 the additive map 1−π^(−d)σ^h:E†→E† is surjective. A solution to (1−π^(−d)σ^h)y=x is y=−Σₘ≥1 π^(dm)σ^(−hm)(x); the same formula is valid on the completion and is compatible with inclusion.

proofSteps: Backward Frobenius reduces residue-coefficient growth by q^(−hm), while π^(dm) gives a linearly increasing integral valuation. This produces one positive convergence radius for the tail: if r·v_k(x)+k≥C for all k, then each term π^(dm)σ^(−hm)(x) satisfies the same bound with C+dm in place of C.
Telescope finite partial sums; their remaining error tends to zero in the analytic and π-adic topologies.
This is the FF coefficient/iterate transport of the imported negative-slope rank-one cohomology, not a new claim of Ext vanishing in both slope directions.

nodes.title: Isoclinic completion comparison
nodes.statement: For two E† Frobenius modules of the same prescribed arithmetic slope λ, completion induces a bijection on Frobenius-linear morphisms. If F is algebraically closed, the completion functor on slope-λ objects is an equivalence, with standard blocks providing essential surjectivity. For a general perfect F, only full faithfulness is asserted here.

SFR Remark 6.3.4 shows that essential surjectivity fails in general; it is asserted here only for algebraically closed F. Mixed-slope Homs do not reduce to unit root.

In equal characteristic E=F_q((π)), the coefficient Frobenius fixes π; comparison with Hartl–Pink uses π as their z and coefficientwise q-power σ.
hypotheses: F is algebraically closed complete nontrivially valued of characteristic p; coefficient field E is either FF mixed characteristic or F_q((π)).
The Banach charts, their overlap restrictions and φ-rescaling maps must be supplied by RD.0; equal-characteristic coefficients are Laurent series in π with coefficients in F.
proofSteps: Spread a finitely presented module and Frobenius isomorphism to one small annular chart.
Translate that chart by Frobenius powers, glue across intersections using the isomorphism and its cocycle, and restrict back to recover the germ.
Match the FF norms and HP Laurent convergence conditions chartwise. This match and the mixed-characteristic extension are G3; a mere coincidence of symbols R is not a ring identification.

nodes.title: Equal-characteristic extension section theorem
nodes.statement: Over the Hartl–Pink punctured-disc ring, for every r≥1 and every σ-bundle extension 0→O(−1)→G→F_(1,r)→0 there is a nonzero Frobenius-fixed section of G.
hypotheses: F is complete algebraically closed characteristic p with nontrivial norm; σ is coefficientwise q-power, fixes the Laurent variable z.
HP F_(d,r) has σ^r=z^(−d), geometric degree d and arithmetic slope −d/r.
proofSteps: Write the extension matrix [[z,b],[0,A_(1,r)]]. A section of the quotient has coordinates v_t=Σᵢ∈ℤz^(−i)w^(q^(ir−t)) for 0<|w|<1; the first coordinate u must solve u=zσ(u)+bσ(v).
Its forced coefficients are u_i=Σⱼ≥0 f_(i−j)^(q^j). The negative-power tail always converges; the positive tail is controlled by a fractional q-polynomial condition (HP Lemmas 9.3–9.4).

Reduce to HP Proposition 9.5. Discard residue-norm ≤1 coefficients and shift so m=Σ_l m_l z^l has only positive exponents, with log|m_l|≤cl. For n=r+1 form F_i(w)=Σ_(0<j<ni)F_(i,j)w^(q^(−j)), where F_(i,j)=Σ_(j/n<k≤i)m_(nk−j)^(q^(−k)). Their logarithmic profiles φ_(i,j)=log|F_(i,j)| satisfy φ_(i+l,j+nl)=q^(−l)φ_(i,j); the actual coefficient differences satisfy log|F_(i′,j)−F_(i,j)|≤cn i q^(−i) for i′≥i≥2.
If every limiting φ_j≤0, any sufficiently small nonzero w works. Otherwise choose a corner ρ≥cn of max_j(φ_j−q^(−j)ρ), with positive maximum at two j. Newton polygons yield roots w_i of norm exp(−ρ).

Use the ball-image criterion for additive fractional q-polynomials to choose compatible roots with log|w_(i+1)−w_i|≤−c′q^((n−1)i/2). Their limit w retains nonzero norm; splitting j at ni/2 gives limsup log|F_i(w)|≤0 and the required positive-tail convergence.

nodes.title: Equal-characteristic Frobenius classification
nodes.statement: For algebraically closed perfectoid F and E=F_q((π)), every finite projective Frobenius module over R_F is a direct sum of standard blocks with coprime integer pair (c,r), r>0, satisfying φ^r=π^c. The multiset of pairs is unique, and its arithmetic slope is c/r. With c=−d these are the Hartl–Pink blocks F_(d,r). Together with the imported mixed-characteristic classification, this covers the two coefficient characteristics in FF Remark 11.3.4, subject to the explicit ring comparison G3.
hypotheses: The precise coefficient category is the one in frobenius-germ-extension, not a completion-only bounded category.
Do not assume finite projective underlying modules on a nonspherically complete punctured disc are free before σ-bundle classification.
proofSteps: Use HP Theorem 4.1 to find a line subbundle of maximal degree; saturation and the degree bound make its quotient a σ-bundle. Rank-one classification and slope-ordered splitting are the imported standard/HN inputs transported to this coefficient category (G3).

Induct simultaneously: every degree-zero bundle has a section; every bundle splits into standard blocks; every nonnegative-degree bundle has a section. The nonsplit degree-zero obstruction is equalchar-degree-zero-section-input.

For rank r and degree d, pull back under [r] and twist by −d to obtain degree zero. A section yields a map from [r]_*O(d). If full rank, use saturation/degree and gcd(d,r); otherwise split off a standard summand by the slope inequality and induct.
HP Corollary 11.8 gives uniqueness. Transport through the germ comparison, preserving the sign c=−d and arithmetic slope convention.

sources.match: The classification adds equal-characteristic coefficients without rebuilding the already planned standard-block notion.

nodes.title: Common Newton-vertex subisocrystal
nodes.statement: Let X be a smooth variety over a perfect field k of characteristic p, with an F^n-bearing convergent isocrystal E and a common Newton-polygon vertex of horizontal coordinate a at every geometric point. Then there is a unique convergent Frobenius subisocrystal of rank a whose slopes are the smallest a slopes at each point.
hypotheses: Finite coefficient field, fixed n≥1 and a fixed common break; use the convergent category, not merely a differential module or an arbitrary overconvergent subobject.
proofSteps: At the generic point use classical Dieudonné–Manin to select the initial slope block.
Extend the corresponding subobject across the base by the common-vertex theorem; this uses the curve/Katz purity arguments named in Notes Theorem 4.1, not just generic linear algebra (G4).

A connection respects the block because its second fundamental map goes from lower slopes to higher slopes and the relevant Frobenius Hom is zero (Notes Remark 4.5). Uniqueness follows from the same slope separation.

sources.match: A common vertex is the global extension input for a constant-Newton-polygon slope filtration.

Neither this theorem nor its application asserts that the filtration lies in the overconvergent category.

nodes.title: Dense-open global slope filtration
nodes.statement: For an F^n-bearing convergent isocrystal on a smooth variety X over perfect k, there is a dense open U whose complement is a divisor such that on each connected component of U the Newton polygon is constant and the isocrystal has a unique filtration with isoclinic graded pieces of strictly increasing slopes.
hypotheses: X is smooth of finite type; coefficients and F^n are fixed as in common-vertex-global-subobject.
An empty divisor is allowed; disconnected components are treated separately.
proofSteps: Upper semicontinuity and purity of the Newton-jumping locus give a dense open constant-polygon locus with complement of pure codimension one (Notes Theorem 3.12). On regular X this is the support of a divisor. The proof of this purity supplier is G4.
For each successive vertex use the common-vertex theorem, then pass to its quotient.
The first graded piece has the smallest slope. Frobenius-Hom vanishing gives compatibility and uniqueness; the result is global on U and distinct from the local Robba slope filtration of RD.2.

nodes.title: de Jong reverse slope filtration
nodes.statement: For M† over E†_alg, write the completed increasing slope filtration 0=S₀⊂S₁⊂…⊂Sₘ=M. There is a unique reverse filtration 0=Srev₀⊂…⊂Srevₘ=M† whose i-th graded piece completes to S_(m+1−i)/S_(m−i), for 1≤i≤m. If M† is isoclinic of slope s/r then, after possibly replacing (s,r) by (ks,kr) for a positive integer k, M†[p^(1/r)] has a Frobenius eigenbasis with eigenvalue p^(s/r); this applies to each isoclinic grade.
hypotheses: E†_alg is the fraction field of the subring of W(k(t)^alg) of Teichmüller series Σ[fᵢ]pⁱ whose t-adic valuations v(fᵢ) are bounded below by a linear function of i (D'Addezio Definition 4.2.5); k is perfect, the residue field k(t)^alg is algebraically closed but not complete, and E_alg is the p-adic completion. Slope indices begin at 0.
s∈ℤ, r>0; negative s is allowed; the coefficient extension and Frobenius lift fix the chosen scalar eigenvalue.
proofSteps: Apply the descending generic filtration over the completed extended ring (SFR Proposition 5.4.3, as in descending-generic-filtration) and intersect back to E†_alg using O_(E^alg)[p^(1/b)]∩Γ_(2,b,c)=O†_(E^alg)[p^(1/b)] (D'Addezio, proof of Theorem 4.2.6, p. 15); this ring comparison is part of G3. Compare its graded completions with the ascending filtration in reverse order.
Uniqueness identifies the grade as S_(m+1−i)/S_(m−i). The printed shifted indices in D’Addezio are corrected; at i=m the quotient is S₁/S₀.
For one isoclinic grade apply classical standard-block classification and fixed-slope full faithfulness after the finite scalar extension to transport the Frobenius eigenbasis.

nodes.title: Robba kernel–cokernel residue pairing
nodes.statement: For a finite free differential Robba module M over L with coordinate T and connection operator ∂ for δ=(1+T)d/dT, define H¹_∂(M)=coker ∂ and H⁰_∂(M∨)=ker ∂∨. The pairing sends ([m],ℓ) to Res_T(⟨m,ℓ⟩ dT/(1+T)). For δ=d/dT the one-form is dT instead. The dual connection is determined by δ⟨m,ℓ⟩=⟨∂m,ℓ⟩+⟨m,∂∨ℓ⟩.
hypotheses: L is a complete characteristic-zero nonarchimedean coefficient field; the Robba derivative has zero residue on exact one-forms.
For the Dospinescu–Le Bras convention ∇=t(1+T)d/dT on coefficients and ∂=t⁻¹∇, t=log(1+T).
The dual is the differential-module dual. For N_rig(V̌), V̌=V*⊗χ_cyc, choose the horizontal generator t⁻¹e_χ of N_rig(L(1)) to identify it with this dual.

For horizontal ℓ the value on ∂m is the residue of δ⟨m,ℓ⟩ dT/(1+T)=d⟨m,ℓ⟩, hence zero. Descend to the additive/L-linear cokernel.

Export the pairing of quotient classes; changes of coordinate act on the differential form, not just on the scalar coefficient. The cyclotomic twist is fixed by the horizontal generator, without an extra claim of φ/Γ-equivariance.

nodes.title: Robba residue duality
nodes.statement: For a finite free differential module with a compatible invertible Frobenius structure over R_L, where L is complete discretely valued of characteristic zero with perfect residue field of characteristic p>0 and a q-Frobenius lift, H⁰ and H¹ for its connection are finite-dimensional, and the residue pairing H¹_∂(M)×H⁰_∂(M∨)→L is perfect. In the DLB convention, this identifies N_rig(V)/∂N_rig(V) with the L-dual of N_rig(V̌)^(∂=0) after the horizontal Tate-line identification.
hypotheses: The Frobenius and finite-dimensional module hypotheses are essential to the public local-monodromy proof route.
Use the same one-form/derivation and differential dual as residue-duality-pairing; no bare representation-dual identification.
This theorem uses the discretely valued positive-residue-characteristic hypotheses of RD.2 local monodromy; in the DLB consumer L is a finite extension of Q_p.
proofSteps: Use the imported RD.2 finite-étale local-monodromy and logarithmic-form targets to obtain, after a finite extension, a unipotent model d+A du/u with A nilpotent. This is a theorem dependency on RD.2, not a redeveloped quasi-unipotence theorem.

Integrate Laurent coefficients of nonzero degree; polynomial-size denominators preserve convergence on a smaller annulus. H⁰ is ker A and H¹ is coker A. The residue pairing is the evaluation coker A × ker Aᵗ, hence perfect by finite-dimensional linear algebra.
Use finite-cover trace and pullback with their degree normalisation to descend perfectness to L. The analytic normal-form and trace comparison details remain G5.

As a consumer check, for a two-dimensional absolutely irreducible nontrianguline de Rham V, DLB Lemma 6.3 gives ∂-injectivity using t^hN⊂D_rig and (∇−h)(t^hx)=t^(h+1)∂x. Apply the same result to V̌ and perfectness for surjectivity, giving Proposition 6.4. The representation/N_rig construction itself is outside RD.1.
